title: From CLI to PR: Automating the path to merged code | BRK203

segments.text: Cassidy Williams: Hello everybody.
Good morning.
Evan Boyle: Morning.
Cassidy Williams: Good morning.
There we go.
Happy, what day is it?
Tuesday? Wednesday?
Wednesday.
Oh my goodness.
It has been a busy build.
But we're very excited to talk with you about the CLI today.
So this is all about migrating your code,
getting to merged code with the CLI.
My name is Cassidy Williams and I am
on the Developer Advocacy Team at GitHub.
Evan Boyle: Hi.
I'm Evan Boyle.
I'm the Engineering Manager for the CLI team.
Cassidy Williams: And we have a bit
of an agenda for you today.
We will do slides to talk about parts of the CLI
that we think that you should know.
And then we're going to get right
into actually building things with code.
And we'll have some audience interaction.
You guys can shout out what you want to learn about.
Okay. So first of all, so many people are using AI tools
and agents more than ever.
Where last year, we made a really big deal about it
where we crossed the billion-commit mark.
It was exciting.
But now we're hitting about 275 million per week,
and that was just the last number I heard.
It's probably even more than that.
We're getting so many commits.
And that number is astronomical.
But as a result, you need to figure out how
to get code landed where it's not just committing code,
but getting code actually merged into a pull request
and from a pull request.
So how it does get merged is typically there is a workflow
that happens where a developer picks an issue and then
from there, they start, in their AI tool of choice
to explore, to scaffold whatever they want to do.
They got to push to a branch, they got to open a pull request,
they have to get a code review,
they have to get everything CI validated.
And then merged once everyone is happy.
And you've probably seen this kind of workflow before.
Sometimes there's an AI tool of choice,
sometimes there is just opening up in VS Code or something.
But more and more, once again,
we're seeing developers using these AI tools to do so.
And we're hoping that that AI tool
of choice can be a GitHub Copilot tool.
But today we're going
to be specifically talking about, once again, the CLI.
Now, the CLI is fun because it's a headless thing that can power,
for example, the GitHub Copilot app.
It can power the various SDKs and tools
that you might want to use.
But there's some particularly cool features that we wanted
to talk about, and then we can go
into any specific details you want to hear about.
So first of all, it does have code generation.
You can interact with it.
You can choose which models that you want to use.
It has automations.
It has a lot of really nice slash commands that allow you
to customize your experience in your terminal.
It has access to all the latest models.
In fact, I don't think this slide is even accurate anymore
because the models come out so often.
But you can choose your model with simply a slash command
and say, "Okay, I want to just do auto mode
where you pick a model for me.
I want to choose the more small models to do some initial work
and then go to larger models when I want to do planning."
But you have access to all the latest models from Anthropic,
OpenAI, and Gemini, and you're able to interact
with them as you wish.
You also have access to the ability to add skills.
And so you can add skills where, for example, let's just say,
you have an accessibility skill where you say, "Okay,
this is specifically an accessibility-driven
agent skill."
You can use ones that are compatible
with Claude Code or with the CLI.
It can read from both folders, the .cot or the .copilot folder.
And it can have access to various MCP servers and tools.
You could say, "Okay, I want you to give me screenshots
of the differences every single time I make a frontend change."
For example, and it can put that in a pull request.
And it also has built-in agents.
And so you can have your custom ones which are very similar
to skills but with access to a bit more tools.
But the built-in agents allow you to interact with a codebase,
explore a codebase, and get a lay of the land.
There's also a custom agent for actually running tasks
and saying, "Okay, I want you
to implement this feature, do that."
The review agent is my favorite.
I skipped the general.
But the review agent, I think, is really great
because it just finds holes in your codebase.
Just the Copilot Code Review agent alone is the number three
contributor to GitHub's codebase.
Because all it does is find security issues, bugs,
any sorts of improvements that need to be made,
it makes those contributions.
And then, yeah, the general agent
that does all of the other things.
Now in terms of modes in the CLI, I love plan mode.
Plan mode is my favorite thing.
And so when you get into the CLI,
which once again will show you, you can hit "Shift Tab"
and when you "Shift Tab" in the CLI, it can shift
between all the different modes.
And so there's regular mode
where you can ask something that's very interactive back
and forth, and then plan mode, that,
you talk about what you want to build.
It could be in an existing codebase,
it could be in a fresh, new codebase.
And as you say what you want to do, what you want to build,
it'll ask you questions about that, and vet your plan
until you have a fully-working plan together with SQL to-dos
and everything where you can interact with that plan
and figure out, okay, do I want to implement this?
Do I want to edit this?
What holes are there?
You can have multiple documentation and everything.
Am I missing anything with plan mode?
It's great.
Evan Boyle: I think with plan mode, the most important thing
for me, if I'm building a non-trivial feature,
I always start in plan mode.
And often, it's an hour plus.
If you have a clear spec for a complicated feature,
if you align on the agent, you understand the architecture,
you agree with the plan.
I'll do web research, I'll go look at open source repos.
I'll search for NPM packages
or Rust crates that might be useful.
I spend a lot of time in plan mode.
Once I'm in plan mode, I shift into autopilot
and I one shot my implementation about 95% of the time.
Cassidy Williams: And it's really just specification driven
where if you like to get your hands on the code,
it's a little bit different of a workflow, but what's great
about plan mode is because you get all of those specifications,
you know exactly what is going to be built.
So you don't have to worry so much about the syntax
of the individual pieces of code that you're writing.
And you care more about the features
that are being implemented, how they're being implemented based
on the research that you've put in.
And you don't have to just write text in there,
you can paste images in the CLI, and it'll put in different pads.
There have been times where I put in pads
for different folders or different files on my machine.
I'll even paste in a PDF, and it can parse that, and you can use
that as context as you're building things.
We have a few different features that we put in individually
of just our favorite CLI features.
Evan, you put your features in first
so I'll let you start with those.
Evan Boyle: Yeah, "/review".
So this lets you run subagents that do code review.
The coolest things about this is
because Copilot is a multi-model harness,
we support Gemini models, we support GPT, Claude,
all the latest and greatest.
And so if you type, "/review" you can give it a prompt
at the end.
My favourite prompt is "/review use GPT-5.5, Sonnet 4.6,
and Gemini all in parallel to do a code review."
When you ask that, it'll spin up three subagents and they get
to duke it out, right?
You get the highest-quality code review.
It helps eliminate the noise.
The outer model gets to, kind of, collect all of that feedback
and then go research and validate it.
"/new" is a new one.
So we've actually turned the CLI into a session manager itself.
So when you run "/new" it'll create a new CLI process
and then you can list them, switch between them.
Many of you might use CLI coding agents and Tmux.
I've seen people with huge monitors
and nine terminals spread out across it.
You can now accomplish that same workflow with "/new"
And then finally, "/pr", one of my favorites.
This one lets you open pull requests, manage pull requests.
There's an "Auto fix" subcommand within PR
so that whenever there are CI failures or you get feedback
from Copilot Code Review, it'll auto-resolve that for you.
This is really helpful when you're juggling more work,
if you have a high confidence change, and you know, "Hey,
I just got to make this green.
I know I have this coworker who's going to ask me
to refactor this function from 250 lines to 200
and I'm just going to say okay so I get that green check."
"Auto-fix" is great for that.
Cassidy Williams: I also really like "Fleet".
"Fleet" lets you run multiple subagents at once.
And so for example, what Evan was saying with the review,
what you can do with "Fleet" is you can say, "I want you to do
that at the exact same time."
What I've often done in plan mode actually is I do "/fleet"
and I say, "I want you to come up with a test plan
for this particular feature and I want you to do it with Gemini,
with the Claude models, with the Opus models."
And you could also pull in a model from Foundry
if you have one or you have something with BYOK,
Bring Your Own Key, "Give me all of them in parallel and then
at the end, come up with a plan that has been vetted
by all of the agents."
And so you can do that in plan mode, you could do
that in conjunction with "Review".
It's nice to just get multiple things running
at the exact same time.
Or if you've done an entire plan, you could say,
"Implement everything with fleet."
And you could see all of them running at the same time
and then just have everything done at the end
and you can see what the different individual models did.
And then "Research"
and "Experimental" are actually new, right?
Those ones are pretty cool --
Evan Boyle: Yeah.
So "Research" is really incredible.
It uses this technology at GitHub called Blackbird
which is our code search engine.
So Blackbird has access to search every open-source repo,
all of your private repos.
And so "Research" will generate an extensive report on a topic.
It could be, "Hey, what's the best load balancer tech
to use in 2026?"
It'll even provide citations at the bottom of the report.
And then it gives you the option at the end to export
that to a gist so you can share it with your coworkers.
"/experimental", this is where we put all of the fun,
new things that we're trying out that we want feedback
on before they go into main line.
So for instance, "Research", "Fleet", "Review", "PR",
all these features started out in
"Experimental" while we were gathering feedback,
getting bake time.
So if you're a person who loves to live on the bleeding edge,
I suggest you crack open your laptop now
and run "/experimental" on.
Cassidy Williams: It's been really fun to use that one.
What I really loved in "Experimental", and I think it's
out now, is "Voice mode".
That one was so cool, where you can actually verbally speak
to the CLI and it has a cool visualization and stuff.
But then it is really, it's speech to text, but in the CLI,
and it's built in, and that was really cool.
And then speaking of "Voice mode", that is new,
the CLI now where it's passed the experimental flag.
So you can use it whenever you want.
I have found more and more how comfortable I am with voice mode
in general across all of the different surfaces
and even outside of the CLI where I love being able
to just say what I want because my voice is a little bit faster
than typing.
And luckily, if you stumble over your words and everything,
the agents get it, and so you don't have
to say everything absolutely perfectly.
You could say, "I want to the implement this, and actually,
I want to do this and this and this.
Scratch that last thing."
And it'll parse it, it'll understand it,
and you can work with it.
The "rubber-duck" feature is also one where if you were
in the keynote yesterday, I showed that a little bit
in the GitHub Copilot app.
But "rubber-duck" lets you consult other agent families
or other AI model families
because every single AI model has a bias of some kind
because that's just the nature of things.
And we found it a statistically significant improvement
if you use "rubber-duck"
to ask another model family how you can improve a specific plan.
This was a big question that I got a few times yesterday.
You can do this with the powerful Claude Opus 4.8 latest
and greatest.
You could also do it with Claude Haiku from GPT-4 or 4.5 Mini.
It works across model families no matter what,
from small to big models.
And it's really, really awesome.
Could you speak to "Every"?
Evan Boyle: Yeah, "/every".
So this is a feature in which you can, within a session,
create an automation that runs on a particular interval.
Could be every five minutes, once a day, once an hour.
My favourite feature of "Every" is that at GitHub,
we live across Slack and Teams and we use lots
of different communication channels.
It's honestly really hard to keep up with when you have email,
two different chat clients, you have public, private repos
that you're monitoring issues from.
And so I use "/every" with a bunch of different MCPs
to produce an hourly report of, "Hey, give me links
to the top ten messages that I need
to go respond to right now."
So rather than me having to sift through hundreds and hundreds
of things, "Every" tells me exactly what are the ten things
I need to go and look at now.
Cassidy Williams: Yeah, it's really nice.
I have a bunch of automations.
I've been moving more and more to the app,
but it's the exact same thing
because the app is powered by the CLI.
And being able to just say, "Okay, every single week,
I want a changelog summary of all the things that were merged
in a particular codebase."
Is really nice to be able to have that so you don't have
to handwrite everything or remember everything.
Now, also new in the CLI is the new TUI,
Terminal User Interface.
That's the hot, new lingo there.
But the new TUI basically is a whole new user interface
that you can access today, right?
Is it beyond the experimental flag?
Evan Boyle: Yes.

And so --
Evan Boyle: It's out today.

to navigate across different sessions, across PRs,
across various elements of work in one place.
And it's really nice to use.
It feels snazzy.
Also, a very cool thing is in JetBrains,
in the JetBrains IDEs, you can now use the Copilot CLI
in there.
And so it allows you to pick the various agents that you want,
pick the features that you want, and it actually uses those CLI
in your JetBrains tools.
So if you're using JetBrains, that's really cool.
And that's new very recently, I think, as of this week,
which is very exciting.
There's also the GitHub Copilot SDK.
And the SDK is built on top of the CLI
so you can build the experience that you want powered by the CLI
in whatever user interfaces you want.
And that has been particularly fun to play with.
And I've got some fun little examples here that we can zoom

tools in your Office softwares, chat interfaces that you want.

And so you don't have to deal with the AI integration side
of building AI tools if you want something to be powered
by the CLI on your computer.
And I thought this one was particularly fun.
